+L45: # Governor Hochul Announces First-in-the-nation Law Requiring Disclosure When Advertisements Include AI-generated Synthetic Performers is in Effect
+L46: 
+L47: Governor Hochul Announces First-in-the-nation Law Requiring Disclosure When Advertisements Include AI-generated Synthetic Performers is in Effect
+L48: 
+L49: Protects Consumers and Boosts Transparency in Advertising in the Film and Television Industry
+L50: Governor Kathy Hochul today announced that the first-in-the-nation law to boost AI transparency in advertising in the film and television industry is now in effect. The law, signed in December 2025, requires persons who produce or create an advertisement to identify if it includes AI-generated synthetic performers.
+L51: “In New York, we are setting the rules of the road instead of letting AI run the show,” Governor Hochul said. “Requiring simple, honest disclosure when an ad uses synthetic performers protects consumers, respects our creative workforce and keeps New York at the forefront of responsible innovation.”
+L52: AI-generated synthetic performers are digitally-created media that appear as a real person. AI-generated synthetic performers are sometimes used by advertisers to sell products, and with easy access to technology, there has been an increase in the use of AI-generated performers across all forms of media, including on social media and in digital advertising.
+L53: Without notice that the content the public is viewing is not real, AI-generated synthetic performers and manipulated media can undermine one's ability to accurately distill fact from fiction.
+L54: State Senator Michael Gianaris said, “Film and television production remains an integral part of New York’s economy, and that is why New York will continue to lead in protecting the workers who power this industry. As this legislation goes into effect, New York’s performers will be better protected from their likenesses being deceptively replaced by artificial intelligence, and we can hold accountable those who would take advantage of these tools to profit improperly at the expense of the real talent.
+L55: Thank you to Governor Hochul for enacting this important law.”
+L56: Assemblymember Linda B. Rosenthal (D/WF - Manhattan) said, “The rise of deepfakes and AI-generated performers have made it more difficult than ever for consumers to decipher fact from fiction. The synthetic performer legislation will alert New Yorkers to the use of synthetic performers in advertisements, providing much-needed transparency to consumers and protections to artists.
+L57: As companies rely on new marketing strategies to sell their products and services, consumers have a right to know if the person featured in those ads is real or fake and our first-in-the-nation law will ensure that happens."
+L58: SAG-AFTRA Chief Labor Policy Officer and New York Local Executive Director Rebecca Damon said, “SAG-AFTRA is grateful to Governor Hochul for placing New York at the forefront of developing smart guardrails around the use of generative AI. This Synthetic Advertisement Disclosure law protects consumers and workers from the risks posed by rapidly developing AI technologies.
+L59: The law’s enforceable protections mitigate performance replacement, prevent consumer deception, and affirm the continued value of human performance. As artificial intelligence technology evolves, we look forward to continuing to work with Governor Hochul on further AI guardrails.”
+L60: The enactment of synthetic performer law complements Governor Hochul’s ongoing efforts to ensure that the use of AI is for the common good. As technology continues to evolve, Governor Hochul remains committed to keeping New Yorkers safe online, and has implemented nation-leading regulations to ensure safe and responsible AI use in New York State. Initiatives include:
+L61:   * The SAFE for Kids Act and Child Data Protection Act that restrict addictive feeds for kids and prevent online operators from collecting and monetizing children’s data without informed consent.
+L62:   * AI Companion legislation which set first-in-the-nation safeguards, diverting user conversations about self-harm to mental health resources and interrupting unhealthy addictive behaviors. The Governor also outlawed AI-Generated Child Sexual Abuse Material.
+L63:   * The Unplug and Play Agenda which helps encourage healthy socialization and child development by funding social infrastructure, physical sites like playgrounds, community centers, and pools, and expanded youth programming.
+L64:   * New York’s Distraction Free Learning Policy which is already resulting in greater academic achievement, improved student wellbeing, and safer school environments for students.
+L65:   * The recently signed Warning Labels bill that will require social media companies post warnings about the platform's potential impact on mental health.
+L66:   * AI Deceptive Practices Act, which enhances protections against unauthorized use of likeness/voice and the unauthorized dissemination of intimate images.
+L67: This year, the Governor’s Safe by Design Act was implemented in the FY27 State Budget. Safe by Design ensures that parental controls for kids are set at the highest protections on common social and gaming platforms, which means that non-connections above the age of 18 cannot privately communicate with kids, view their full profile, or tag them in content. Location settings will also be turned off by default, and children under 13 must receive parental approval for new connections.
+L68: It also disables certain AI chatbot features on online platforms for kids and parents must be able to set limits on children’s financial transactions on online gaming platforms and view their child’s transaction history. While many of these platforms have increased their security features for kids, in New York it is now the law, and cannot be relaxed by these platforms over time.
+L69: Additionally, Governor Hochul is now creating a first-of-its kind Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity, and Trust (DIGIT). DIGIT will serve as a central, authoritative body for digital safety and technological governance, devising new approaches and ensuring consistent enforcement to keep New Yorkers safe online; while protecting New York’s position as a state that values and invests in cutting edge innovation.
+L70: The DIGIT Office will first focus on regulating large frontier AI developers, enabling greater transparency into their safety measures and establishing a reporting mechanism for developers to report critical safety incidents.

+L50: ## SECTION 396-B
+L51: 
+L52: ### Advertisements
+L53: #### General Business (GBS) CHAPTER 20, ARTICLE 26
+L54: § 396-b. Advertisements. 1. For the purposes of this section, the
+L55: following terms shall have the following meanings:
+L56: (a) "Artificial intelligence", "artificial intelligence technology",
+L57: or "AI" means a machine-based system that can, for a given set of
+L58: human-defined objectives, make predictions, recommendations, or
+L59: decisions influencing real or virtual environments, and that uses
+L60: machine- and human-based inputs to perceive real and virtual
+L61: environments, abstract such perceptions into models through analysis in
+L62: an automated manner, and use model inference to formulate options for
+L63: information or action. This definition includes but is not limited to
+L64: systems that use machine learning, large language model, natural
+L65: language processing, and computer vision technologies, including
+L66: generative artificial intelligence.
+L67: (b) "Generative artificial intelligence" means a class of artificial
+L68: intelligence models that are self-supervised and emulate the structure
+L69: and characteristics of input data to generate derived synthetic content,
+L70: including, but not limited to, images, videos, audio, text, and other
+L71: digital content.
+L72: (c) "Synthetic performer" means a digitally created asset created,
+L73: reproduced, or modified by computer, using generative artificial
+L74: intelligence or a software algorithm, that is intended to create the
+L75: impression that the asset is engaging in an audiovisual and/or visual
+L76: performance of a human performer who is not recognizable as any
+L77: identifiable natural performer.
+L78: 2. Any person, firm, corporation or association, or agent or employee
+L79: thereof, hereinafter called person, who, being engaged in the business
+L80: of dealing in any property, makes, publishes, disseminates, circulates
+L81: or places before the public or causes, directly or indirectly, to be
+L82: made, published, disseminated, circulated or placed before the public,
+L83: in this state, any advertisement respecting any such property, in any
+L84: newspaper, magazine, or other publication, or over any radio station or
+L85: television station, unless it is stated in any such advertisement that
+L86: the advertiser is a dealer in such property or from the context of any
+L87: such advertisement, it plainly appears that such person is a dealer in
+L88: such property so offered for sale in any such advertisement; or when
+L89: placing or causing any such advertisement to appear in any newspaper,
+L90: magazine or other publication or radio or television station as
+L91: described in this section, if requested by the publisher of any such
+L92: newspaper, magazine or other publication or owner or operator of such
+L93: radio or television station or any agent or representative thereof to
+L94: file with such owner or operator, publisher, agent or representative
+L95: thereof such person's true name, or where such person is transacting
+L96: business under a name other than the true name pursuant to law, then the
+L97: name under which such business is transacted, and each business address
+L98: wherein any business is transacted by such person, in the class of
+L99: property advertised or to be advertised for sale in such advertisement,
+L100: shall make any false statement in relation to any of such items; or if
+L101: requested by the publisher of any such newspaper, magazine or other
+L102: publication or owner or operator of such radio or television station or
+L103: any agent or representative thereof to file with such owner, operator,
+L104: publisher, agent or representative thereof a statement showing whether
+L105: such person is causing such advertisement to appear or is offering to
+L106: make such sale or disposition or transaction, as herein set forth, as
+L107: principal or agent, and if as agent, to set forth such information as is
+L108: specified in this section, in relation to such person's principal as
+L109: well as in relation to such person, shall make any false statement in
+L110: relation to any of such items; is guilty of a misdemeanor.
+L111: 3. Any person engaged in the business of dealing in any property or
+L112: service who for any commercial purpose produces or creates an
+L113: advertisement respecting any such property or service, in any medium or
+L114: media in which such advertisement appears, shall conspicuously disclose
+L115: in such advertisement that a synthetic performer is in such
+L116: advertisement, where such person has actual knowledge. A violation of
+L117: this subdivision shall result in a civil penalty of one thousand dollars
+L118: for a first violation, and five thousand dollars for any subsequent
+L119: violation.
+L120: 4. This section shall not apply to advertisements and promotional
+L121: materials for expressive works, including but not limited to, motion
+L122: pictures, television programs, streaming content, documentaries, video
+L123: games, or other similar audiovisual works, provided that the use of a
+L124: synthetic performer in the advertisement or promotional material is
+L125: consistent with its use in the expressive work.
+L126: 5. Nothing in this section shall limit, reduce, or enlarge any rights
+L127: any person may have under section fifty, fifty-f, or fifty-one of the
+L128: civil rights law or under any other law.
+L129: 6. Nothing in this section shall be construed to limit, or to enlarge,
+L130: the protections that 47 U.S.C. section 230 confers on an interactive
+L131: computer service for content provided by another information content
+L132: provider, as such terms are defined in 47 U.S.C. section 230.
+L133: 7. This section shall not apply to advertisements and promotional
+L134: materials in any of the following circumstances:
+L135: (a) Audio advertisements; or
+L136: (b) Where the use of artificial intelligence solely involves the
+L137: language translation of a human performer.
+L138: 8. Nothing in this section shall apply to any medium used for
+L139: advertising, including, but not limited to, newspapers, magazines, and
+L140: television networks and stations, streaming services, cable television
+L141: systems, billboards, and transit advertisements, by whom any
+L142: advertisement or solicitation in violation of this section is published
+L143: or disseminated.

+---
+title: AI Content for Beauty and Skincare Brands
+slug: ai-content-beauty-skincare
+description: Plan AI beauty content around product evidence: what to generate, how to review skin results, and which market and model disclosure rules apply.
+excerpt: Plan beauty assets around real product evidence, with clear decisions on generated scenes, skin results, synthetic models, market rules, and final approval.
+template: insight
+---
+
+<!-- HERO SECTION -->
+
+# AI content for beauty brands: skincare and claims
+
+Use AI to build a campaign around the product. Keep the product's appearance
+and any result shown on skin tied to evidence, even when the image contains
+no written claim.
+
+By Cyril Drouin
+
+<!-- INTRODUCTION -->
+
+## Where does AI content for beauty brands fit?
+
+AI content for beauty brands can extend settings, casting, and campaign
+variations, provided the finished image represents the product truthfully.
+hubStudio combines generated work with product photography and human review.
+Keep packaging, shades, and texture tied to approved references; use suitable
+evidence for efficacy claims. A generated result is not proof.
+
+Decide what each asset asks a buyer to believe. A bathroom scene
+sets a mood. A cream disappearing into skin suggests absorption. A face with
+fewer visible lines can suggest a result even without a before-and-after
+caption. For a serum launch, commission the setting separately from any
+demonstration of what happens after application.
+
+| Asset | Production choice | Claim risk | Suggested sign-off |
+|---|---|---|---|
+| Packshot | Photograph the current pack; mix with a generated setting if needed | Altered label, shape, quantity, or applicator | Product owner |
+| Texture or shade swatch | Capture the real formula under controlled conditions | Invented finish, color, coverage, or viscosity | Product and claims reviewers |
+| Ingredient visual | Generate a reviewed illustration | Implying an absent ingredient or an unsupported finished-product effect | Claims reviewer |
+| Model campaign | Generate, shoot, or combine, with rights and disclosure review | Skin appearance may imply product performance | Creative and claims reviewers |
+| On-skin result | Use a documented real observation appropriate to the claim | A photograph can still exaggerate or misrepresent results | Evidence owner |
+| Before and after | Use comparable records backed by relevant evidence; never fabricate the result | False improvement or an unrepresentative outcome | Evidence owner and market reviewer |
+
+The sign-off roles are recommendations, not statutory job titles. These
+production choices are not a rule that every asset must be
+shot. The boundary is what the visual communicates, including accurate
+product characteristics as well as efficacy. This article describes
+production practice, not legal advice.
+
+<!-- SECTION: Markets -->
+
+## What do the market rules change about an image?
+
+Rules reviewed October 24, 2026. The market review should happen before the
+creative team settles on a product demonstration. This table identifies the
+rules used here; it is not an exhaustive market-clearance checklist.
+
+| Market | Primary rule or guidance | What to check in the image |
+|---|---|---|
+| US | FDA intended-use definitions; FTC advertising substantiation | Does the picture imply treatment or a body-function change? Does evidence support the overall message? |
+| EU | Cosmetics Regulation Article 20; common claims criteria | Do pictures imply characteristics or functions the product lacks? Does the evidence match the depicted effect? |
+| UK | ASA/CAP beauty-filter guidance | Has a filter or retouch exaggerated the advertised product's effect? |
+| China | NMPA efficacy evaluation standard; local advertising guidance where applicable | Does the visual stay within the product's supported claim and relevant registration or filing information? |
+
+### US: decide whether the claim changes the product's status
+
+The FDA distinguishes cosmetics from drugs by intended use. Cleansing or
+beautifying is different from treating disease or changing the body's
+structure or function. Advertising can help establish that intended use.
+An animation suggesting that a cream rebuilds skin therefore deserves a
+classification review, not just an art director's approval.
+
+> FDA's definitions distinguish appearance-related cosmetic uses from drug
+> uses involving disease or body structure and function. The method is a
+> reading of its intended-use guidance, not a test of an individual product.
+> Source: FDA, September 11, 2024.
+> https://www.fda.gov/cosmetics/cosmetics-laws-regulations/it-cosmetic-drug-or-both-or-it-soap
+
+The FTC separately requires a reasonable basis for objective advertising
+claims before the ad runs, including claims conveyed by implication. If the
+ad communicates that testing proves a result, the support must match that
+message. The team should review image, headline, and caption together.
+
+> Objective advertising claims need prior substantiation, including implied
+> claims. The method is a reading of the FTC's policy on the reasonable-basis
+> requirement and advertised levels of support.
+> Source: Federal Trade Commission, November 23, 1984.
+> https://www.ftc.gov/legal-library/browse/ftc-policy-statement-regarding-advertising-substantiation
+
+### EU: pictures count as claims
+
+Article 20 of the Cosmetics Regulation covers pictures as well as words.
+They cannot imply characteristics or functions the product does not have.
+The common criteria also connect claims to evidence and prevent a depiction
+of performance from going beyond that support.
+
+> Regulation 655/2013 sets six common criteria: legal compliance,
+> truthfulness, evidential support, honesty, fairness, and informed
+> decision-making. The method is a reading of its annex alongside Article 20
+> of Regulation 1223/2009, which expressly includes pictures.
+> Source: European Union, July 10, 2013, and November 30, 2009.
+> https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32013R0655
+> https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32009R1223
+
+An ingredient's documented properties
+do not automatically establish the same effect in the finished formula.
+An illustrated ingredient passing through a skin cross-section may imply
+more than the approved copy says. Give that sequence to the claims reviewer
+before spending time on polished motion.
+
+### UK: a filter can change the claim
+
+The ASA's beauty-filter rulings of February 3, 2021 addressed tanning ads in
+which filters exaggerated the apparent product effect. Its subsequent
+guidance does not prohibit every filter. It asks whether the alteration
+misleads about what the advertised product can achieve.
+
+> A beauty filter becomes a problem when it misleadingly exaggerates product
+> efficacy. The method is a reading of CAP's explanation of the ASA's
+> February 2021 rulings, not a blanket prohibition on retouching.
+> Source: ASA/CAP, February 11, 2021.
+> https://www.asa.org.uk/news/the-mis-use-of-social-media-beauty-filters-when-advertising-cosmetic-products.html
+
+For production, preserve the source footage and record changes to skin tone
+or texture. Removing a distracting object is a different decision from
+smoothing the very lines a moisturizer is advertised to improve.
+
+### China: connect the asset to the claim's evidence
+
+The NMPA efficacy evaluation standard calls for scientific support for
+cosmetic efficacy claims. Evaluation methods depend on the claim. Certain
+sensory and physical-effect claims qualify for an exemption from publishing
+the evidence summary; that does not make a fabricated visual result true.
+
+> The NMPA standard took effect May 1, 2021, with different summary-upload
+> deadlines for products registered or filed at different times. The method is a reading
+> of the complete notice and standard republished by the Yunnan drug
+> regulator, including the summary exemptions.
+> Source: NMPA notice published April 9, 2021; official republication
+> December 22, 2021.
+> https://mpa.yn.gov.cn/zfxxgk/zcwj/qtwj/gjwj/202112/t20211222_1224866.html
+
+Beijing's cosmetics advertising guidance makes the connection explicit:
+efficacy and safety advertising should agree with the relevant registration
+or filing information and evidence summary. That is local guidance, not a
+new nationwide platform rule.
+
+> Beijing's guidance links efficacy and safety advertising to the product
+> record and supporting summary. The method is a reading of the guidance's
+> content-accuracy provisions and its stated Beijing scope.
+> Source: Beijing market and drug regulators, June 27, 2025.
+> https://scjgj.beijing.gov.cn/zwxx/2024zcwj/202506/t20250627_4129056.html
+
+Beauty content production in China covers the local production context in
+more depth. Do not carry an approved claim into another market merely by
+translating its caption.
+
+<!-- SECTION: Synthetic people -->
+
+## Do synthetic models need a separate disclosure review?
+
+Yes. Review whether the person must be identified as synthetic separately
+from whether the product message is true. The requirements depend on where
+the asset appears and what kind of performer it contains.
+
+Amazon's official listing and A+ announcement requires applicable media
+containing photorealistic AI-generated people to carry the
+`contains-synthetic-performer` keyword in the XMP `dc:subject` field before
+upload. The announcement excludes, among other categories, real people who
+were merely altered using AI. It is not a rule to label every edited bottle.
+
+> Amazon's announcement specifies a metadata tag for photorealistic
+> AI-generated people in listings and A+ content across its worldwide stores.
+> The method is a reading of the official announcement and tagging guide.
+> Source: Amazon Seller Central, July 27, 2026; guide checked October 24, 2026.
+> https://sellercentral-europe.amazon.com/seller-forums/discussions/t/ed53566e-9add-4008-a7bd-2bca6f600fee?mons_sel_locale=en_GB
+> https://sellercentral.amazon.com/help/hub/reference/external/GFXHCHYZRGJRBZA5?locale=en-US
+
+New York's rule is already in effect. Its covered ad creators must
+conspicuously disclose synthetic performers when they have actual knowledge
+of their use. Its definition concerns a human-like visual or audiovisual
+performer who is not recognizable as an identifiable natural person;
+audio-only ads and specified other uses have exclusions.
+
+> New York's synthetic-performer disclosure rule took effect June 9, 2026.
+> The method is a reading of General Business Law 396-b and the governor's
+> dated commencement announcement.
+> Source: New York State, June 9, 2026; statute checked October 24, 2026.
+> https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/GBS/396-B
+> https://www.governor.ny.gov/news/governor-hochul-announces-first-nation-law-requiring-disclosure-when-advertisements-include-ai
+
+California's forthcoming rule covers prominently featured synthetic
+performers and requires clear disclosure. Its definition includes voice, so
+do not assume an audio ad has the same treatment as in New York.
+
+> California's SB 1050 adds Business and Professions Code 17610. Its
+> January 1, 2027 effective date follows from the September 16, 2026 enactment
+> and the constitutional default for this regular-session statute. The
+> method is a reading of the chaptered law and that effective-date rule.
+> Source: California Legislature, September 16, 2026; Article IV, section 8,
+> in the legislature's August 2022 handbook.
+> https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB1050
+> https://www.senate.ca.gov/sites/senate.ca.gov/files/joint_handbook_2021-22_final.pdf
+
+Platform metadata and a conspicuous disclosure within an ad are separate
+delivery requirements. Check the applicable exclusions before selecting the
+final wording. EU AI
+Act labeling for brand content addresses the separate European framework.
+An AI disclosure tells the audience how content was made. It cannot supply
+missing evidence that the skincare product works.
+
+<!-- SECTION: Channel assets -->
+
+## Which assets belong in each channel's brief?
+
+Define the job before requesting variations. The same model portrait can
+read as campaign casting in a brand film and as a product result beside a
+claim on a shopping page. The placement is part of the review.
+
+| Channel | Suggested asset set | Keep attached to the handoff |
+|---|---|---|
+| Product page or marketplace | Current pack, actual texture or shade references, reviewed use demonstration | Product version, evidence references, applicable synthetic-person metadata |
+| Paid social | Campaign scene, product reveal, approved claim variant | Exact caption, disclosure, destination, and market approval |
+| Organic social | Routine context, ingredient illustration, application education | Approved directions and claim wording; review of the implied result |
+| Brand website or launch film | Campaign setting, reviewed product transformation, cutdowns | Source references, explanation of simulated elements, and cleared claims |
+
+The ecommerce design service page is the service reference for shopping
+assets. The Amazon platform page covers that sales channel. For the broader
+production library, start with Insights and AI image production.
+
+<!-- SECTION: Handoff -->
+
+## What should the reviewer receive before approving a batch?
+
+Send a packet that lets the reviewer compare the finished visual with the
+product and the evidence. Include current pack photography, the formula or
+variant identifier, and approved wording for the intended market. Attach
+the relevant study or evidence reference rather than a general assurance
+that the claim is supported.
+
+For a swatch, include the real reference and the capture conditions. For an
+on-skin result, explain the observation and any image processing. A real
+photo can still be misleading if lighting, pose, makeup, or the selection
+of subjects changes the impression of performance. Photography records a
+frame; it does not by itself establish a product's typical effect.
+
+The claims reviewer should see the final crop with its caption and any
+on-image wording. A close crop that removes context can change what the
+viewer believes. Have the reviewer identify the approved version, then
+reopen review if the team changes the product effect or claim.
+
+After export, check the delivered file's metadata where the destination
+requires it. Do not assume that a resize or format conversion preserved the
+tag. Keep the source reference and review record with the delivery copy.
+
+<!-- SECTION: Cases -->
+
+## What do the beauty case studies demonstrate?
+
+The Noyz case study describes a model trained on fluid physics to depict the
+mist-to-milk transformation, with a master film adapted for channel use.
+That is a production account of a simulated product story, not an
+independent efficacy test.
+
+The age20 case study describes product photography becoming on-model
+campaigns across Asian markets, with regional adaptations. Its published
+account gives a case-specific timing claim, not a turnaround promise for a
+new brief.
+
+> The age20 case study reports product photography becoming on-model
+> campaign imagery in hours. This is hubStudio's published account; it does
+> not supply an independent timing study or a delivery guarantee.
+> Source: hubStudio case study, checked October 24, 2026.
+> https://www.hubstudio.ai/work/age20
+
+For Shiseido RQ PYOLOGY, the case study describes campaign visuals and brand
+video balancing clinical credibility with luxury appeal in China's medical
+aesthetics market. It demonstrates the creative brief and delivered work.
+It does not establish that another product or claim has regulatory approval.
+
+<!-- SECTION: Ways to work -->
+
+## How should a beauty team organize the work in hubStudio?
+
+Use the app when your own team can generate and edit the assets and own the
+review. Keep the approved product references close to the work.
+
+Studio + app suits a brand that wants the studio to produce the work while
+its reviewer approves in Validation. The documented workflow lets a
+teammate or client approve an asset or send it back with a comment; versions
+and comments stay on the same thread. The reviewer makes the claims
+decision. The app does not supply legal clearance.
+
+Studio only is the route for commissioning finished work rather than doing
+the production yourself. Service delivery and approval still take place in
+hubStudio, through Client space or the customer's workspace. In each route,
+name the person responsible for product accuracy and the person authorized
+to approve claims before production starts.
+
+<!-- SECTION: FAQ -->
+
+## Questions beauty teams ask before commissioning
+
+### Can beauty brands use AI-generated images in ads?
+
+Yes, subject to the rules for the market, placement, product, and message.
+Generation can provide a campaign setting or an illustrative scene, but the
+finished ad must not mislead about the product. Review skin appearance,
+packaging, and implied results alongside the copy, then check any applicable
+synthetic-performer disclosure requirement.
+
+### Can I show AI-generated before and after skincare results?
+
+Do not present an invented transformation as a person's real result or as
+proof of efficacy. A synthetic comparison does not establish what the
+formula achieves. If the campaign needs a result demonstration, build it
+around appropriate evidence and comparable real records, and have the
+market reviewer assess the complete presentation before release.
+
+### Do AI models in beauty ads need to be disclosed?
+
+Some uses do. New York has a synthetic-performer advertising rule, California
+has enacted a forthcoming rule, and Amazon requires metadata for applicable
+listing and A+ media. Their scopes differ. Check where the ad reaches
+consumers, whether the performer meets the definition, and which disclosure
+must survive the final export and upload.
+
+### Is AI skin retouching allowed in cosmetics advertising?
+
+There is no universal permission for skin retouching. The UK guidance asks
+whether an alteration exaggerates the advertised product's effect; other
+markets also assess truthful claims and supporting evidence. Keep the
+unaltered source, explain changes to the reviewer, and avoid smoothing or
+recoloring that changes the result the product is supposed to deliver.
+
+### What beauty content can AI make well?
+
+Useful assignments include campaign environments, reviewed ingredient
+illustrations, model-led concepts, and adaptations built around approved
+product photography. Treat these as creative tasks with review, not a
+promise of perfect product fidelity. A shade, label, applicator, or texture
+that affects purchase expectations needs checking against the real product
+before the asset leaves the team.
+
+### How do cosmetics claims rules differ in the EU and the US?
+
+In the US, intended use helps determine whether a product is a cosmetic, a
+drug, or both, while FTC rules govern advertising substantiation. EU
+cosmetics rules expressly address pictures and apply common claims criteria.
+Neither system treats a plausible generated image as evidence of efficacy.
+Check the product's status and the exact visual message for each market.
+
+<!-- CTA -->
+
+## What belongs in your production brief?
+
+Send the product references, intended markets, asset placements, and approved
+claims, together with the evidence owner and final reviewer. Identify which
+images illustrate the campaign and which are meant to show an observed
+product result.
+
+CTA: Send a brief

+## Cleared for use
+
+Use paraphrases in attributed blocks, not lengthy verbatim quotations.
+The six EU criteria can be named. Dates and statute identifiers are legal
+identifiers, not market statistics. The age20 timing may appear only as the
+case study's own published account, never as a new delivery promise.
+
+The article can recommend retaining real product references and recorded
+tests. It must not imply that ordinary photography alone proves efficacy,
+that all before-and-after advertising is nationally banned, that all filters
+are prohibited, or that synthetic-person labeling cures an untrue claim.
+
+## Do not publish
+
+- Adoption shares, conversion lifts, savings, client budgets and rates:
+  unnecessary and no method-supported dataset needed for this decision guide.
+- Blanket permission to generate packaging, texture, shades or ingredient
+  effects: disproved by visual-claim and evidence rules; brief corrected.
+- Every market has one universal AI label: statutes and platform requirements
+  have different scope; describe the checked obligations separately.
+- A product photograph or generated demonstration is efficacy test evidence:
+  no support; distinguish illustration, observation and substantiation.
+- Any claim that the app automatically checks cosmetics law, preserves every
+  required metadata field, or provides a regulated claims database: absent
+  from product documentation.
+- Numerical China platform specs: out of scope, none cleared or planned.
+- Noyz imagery as an independent laboratory finding; age20 as a China-only
+  project; Shiseido's creative brief as evidence of regulatory authorization:
+  all excluded.

+# Claim map before research
+
+Written October 24, 2026, before searches or article copy.
+
+- FDA: intended use distinguishes cosmetic appearance claims from drug claims.
+- FTC: objective express and implied advertising claims need appropriate support.
+- EU: cosmetic claims include pictures; evidence and honesty constrain effects depicted.
+- UK: beauty filters cannot misleadingly exaggerate the advertised product's effect.
+- China: efficacy claims need a scientific basis; evaluate the NMPA standard's exact scope and commencement from official Chinese text.
+- Synthetic performers: establish exact scope and dates in New York and California; distinguish platform disclosure from law and from efficacy evidence.
+- Cases: verify Noyz, age20 and Shiseido RQ PYOLOGY against the approved local data only. Cut any numerical performance inference.
+- App: Validation accepts comments and versions; use only positioning/help facts.
+- Editorial recommendations: identify atmosphere versus product representation, per-channel asset selection, reviewer responsibilities and evidence handoff as proposed production practice, not universal legal requirements.
+- Exclude adoption figures, platform dimensions, client metrics, rates and any unsupported claim. Generated imagery is not experimental proof.
+
+R2 audit will omit identifying commercial result domains under the standing no-competitor rule. Preserve positions and coverage anonymously; retain regulator domains.

+FTC Policy Statement Regarding Advertising Substantiation | Federal Trade Commission (https://www.ftc.gov/legal-library/browse/ftc-policy-statement-regarding-advertising-substantiation)
+citeturn20view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: today; Content type: text/html; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://www.ftc.gov/legal-library/browse/ftc-policy-statement-regarding-advertising-substantiation","lineno":null}); Total lines: 79

+L22: Date
+L23: 
+L24: November 23, 1984
+L25: 
+L26: Appended to Thompson Medical Co., 104 F.T.C. 648, 839 (1984), aff’d, 791 F.2d 189 (D.C. Cir. 1986), cert. denied, 479 U.S. 1086 (1987).
+L27: ## Introduction
+L28: On March 11, 1983, the Commission published a notice requesting comments on its advertising substantiation program.1 To facilitate analysis of the program, the notice posed a number of questions concerning the program's procedures, standards, benefits, and costs, and solicited suggestions for making the program more effective.
+L29: Based on the public comments and the staff's review, the Commission has drawn certain conclusions about how the program is being implemented and how it might be refined to serve better the objective of maintaining a marketplace free of unfair and deceptive acts or practices. This statement articulates the Commission's policy with respect to advertising substantiation.
+L30: ## The Reasonable Basis Requirement
+L31: 
+L32: First, we reaffirm our commitment to the underlying legal requirement of advertising substantiation-that advertisers and ad agencies have a reasonable basis for advertising claims before they are disseminated.
+L33: The Commission intends to continue vigorous enforcement of this existing legal requirement that advertisers substantiate express and implied claims, however conveyed, that make objective assertions about the item or service advertised. Objective claims for products or services represent explicitly or by implication that the advertiser has a reasonable basis supporting these claims. These representations of substantiation are material to consumers.
+L34: That is, consumers would be less likely to rely on claims for products and services if they knew the advertiser did not have a reasonable basis for believing them to be true.2 Therefore, a firm's failure to possess and rely upon a reasonable basis for objective claims constitutes an unfair and deceptive act or practice in violation of Section 5 of the Federal Trade Commission Act.
+L35: ## Standards for Prior Substantiation
+L36: Many ads contain express or implied statements regarding the amount of support the advertiser has for the product claim. When the substantiation claim is express (e.g.., "tests prove", "doctors recommend", and "studies show"), the Commission expects the firm to have at least the advertised level of substantiation.
+L37: Of course, an ad may imply more substantiation than it expressly claims or may imply to consumers that the firm has a certain type of support; in such cases, the advertiser must possess the amount and type of substantiation the ad actually communicates to consumers.
+L38: Absent an express or implied reference to a certain level of support, and absent other evidence indicating what consumer expectations would be, the Commission assumes that consumers expect a "reasonable basis" for claims. The Commission's determination of what constitutes a reasonable basis depends, as it does in an unfairness analysis, on a number of factors relevant to the benefits and costs of substantiating a particular claim.
+L39: These factors include: the type of claim, the product, the consequences of a false claim, the benefits of a truthful claim, the cost of developing substantiation for the claim, and the amount of substantiation experts in the field believe is reasonable. Extrinsic evidence, such as expert testimony or consumer surveys, is useful to determine what level of substantiation consumers expect to support a particular product claim and the adequacy of evidence an advertiser possesses.
+L40: One issue the Commission examined was substantiation for implied claims. Although firms are unlikely to possess substantiation for implied claims they do not believe the ad makes, they should generally be aware of reasonable interpretations and will be expected to have prior substantiation for such claims. The Commission will take care to assure that it only challenges reasonable interpretations of advertising claims.3
+L41: ## Procedures for Obtaining Substantiation
+L42: In the past, the Commission has sought substantiation from firms in two different ways: through industry-wide "rounds" that involved publicized inquiries with identical or substantially similar demands to a number of firms within a targeted industry or to firms in different industries making the same type of claim; and on a case-by-case basis, by sending specific requests to individual companies under investigation.
+L43: The Commission's review indicates that "rounds" have been costly to both the recipient and to the agency and have produced little or no law enforcement benefit over a case-by-case approach.
+L44: The Commission's traditional investigatory procedures allow the staff to investigate a number of firms within an industry at the same time, to develop necessary expertise within the area of investigation, and to announce our activities publicly in circumstances where public notice or comment is desirable. The Commission intends to continue undertaking such law enforcement efforts when appropriate.
+L45: However, since substantiation is principally a law enforcement tool and the Commission's concern in such investigations is with the substantiation in the advertiser's possession, there is little, if any, information that the public could contribute in such investigations. Therefore, the Commission anticipates that substantiation investigations will rarely be made public before they are completed.
+L46: Accordingly, the Commission has determined that in the future it will rely on nonpublic requests for substantiation directed to individual companies via an informal access letter or, if necessary, a formal civil investigative demand. The Commission believes that tailored, firm-specific requests, whether directed to one firm or to several firms within the same industry, are a more efficient law enforcement technique.
+L47: The Commission cannot presently foresee circumstances under which the past approach of industry-wide rounds would be appropriate in the ad substantiation area.
+L48: ## Relevance of Post-Claim Evidence in Substantiation Cases
+L49: The reasonable basis doctrine requires that firms have substantiation before disseminating a claim.
+L50: The Commission has on occasion exercised its discretion, however, to consider supporting materials developed after disseminations The Commission has not previously identified in one document the circumstances in which it may, in its discretion, consider post-claim evidence in substantiation cases.5 Such guidance can serve to clarify the program's actual operation as well as focus consideration of postclaim evidence on cases in which it is appropriate.
+L51: The Commission emphasizes that as a matter of law, firms lacking a reasonable basis before an ad is disseminated violate Section 5 of the FTC Act and are subject to prosecution. The goal of the advertising substantiation requirement is to assure that advertising is truthful, however, and the truth or falsity of a claim is always relevant to the Commission's deliberations.
+L52: Therefore, it is important that the agency retain the discretion and flexibility to consider additional substantiating evidence, not as a substitute for an advertiser's prior substantiation, but rather in the following circumstances:
+L53:   * When deciding, before issuance of a complaint, whether there is a public interest in proceeding against a firm;
+L54:   * When assessing the adequacy of the substantiation an advertiser possessed before a claim was made; and
+L55:   * When deciding the need for or appropriate scope of an order to enter against a firm that lacked a reasonable basis prior to disseminating an advertisement.
+L56: First, using post-claim evidence to evaluate the truth of a claim, or otherwise using such evidence in deciding whether there is a public interest in continuing an investigation or issuing a complaint, is appropriate policy. This does not mean that the Commission will postpone action while firms create post-claim substantiation to prove the truthfulness of claims, nor does it mean that subsequent evidence of truthfulness absolves a firm of liability for failing to possess prior substantiation for a claim.
+L57: The Commission focuses instead on whether existing evidence that claims are true should lead us in the exercise of our prosecutorial discretion to decline to initiate a law enforcement proceeding. If available post-claim evidence proves that the claim is true, issuing a complaint against a firm that may have violated the prior substantiation requirement is often inappropriate, particularly in light of competing demands on the Commission's resources.
+L58: Second, post-claim evidence may indicate that apparent deficiencies in the pre-claim substantiation materials have no practical significance. In evaluating the adequacy of prior substantiation, the Commission will consider only post-claim substantiation that sheds light on pre-existing substantiation. Thus, advertisers will not be allowed to create entirely new substantiation simply because their prior substantiation was inadequate.
+L59: Finally, the Commission may use post-claim evidence in determining the need for or appropriate scope of an order to be entered against a firm that lacked a reasonable basis. Thus, when additional evidence offered for the first time at trial suggests that the claim is true, the Commission may frame a narrower order than if there had been no post-claim evidence.
+L60: The Commission remains committed to the prior substantiation requirement and further believes that these discretionary factors will provide necessary flexibility. The Commission will consider post-claim evidence only in the circumstances listed above. But, whether it will do so in any particular case remains within its discretion.
+L61: ## Self Regulation Groups and Government Agencies
+L62: The Commission traditionally has enjoyed a close working relationship with self regulation groups and government agencies whose regulatory policies have some bearing on our law enforcement initiatives. The Commission will not necessarily defer, however, to a finding by a self-regulation group.
+L63: An imprimatur from a self-regulation group will not automatically shield a firm from Commission prosecution, and an unfavorable determination will not mean the Commission will automatically take issue, or find liability if it does. Rather the Commission will make its judgment independently, evaluating each case on its merits.
+L64: We intend to continue our useful relationships with self-regulation groups and to rely on the expertise and findings of other government agencies in our proceedings to the greatest extent possible.
+L65: By direction of the Commission.

Notwithstanding these variations in approach, the focus of all Commissioners on reasonable interpretations of claims is intended to ensure that advertisers are not required to substantiate claims that were not made.

Section 3.40 only provides a sanction against the introduction of evidence that should have been produced in response to a subpoena, but was not.

+L45: # Governor Hochul Announces First-in-the-nation Law Requiring Disclosure When Advertisements Include AI-generated Synthetic Performers is in Effect
+L46: 
+L47: Governor Hochul Announces First-in-the-nation Law Requiring Disclosure When Advertisements Include AI-generated Synthetic Performers is in Effect
+L48: 
+L49: Protects Consumers and Boosts Transparency in Advertising in the Film and Television Industry
+L50: Governor Kathy Hochul today announced that the first-in-the-nation law to boost AI transparency in advertising in the film and television industry is now in effect. The law, signed in December 2025, requires persons who produce or create an advertisement to identify if it includes AI-generated synthetic performers.
+L51: “In New York, we are setting the rules of the road instead of letting AI run the show,” Governor Hochul said. “Requiring simple, honest disclosure when an ad uses synthetic performers protects consumers, respects our creative workforce and keeps New York at the forefront of responsible innovation.”
+L52: AI-generated synthetic performers are digitally-created media that appear as a real person. AI-generated synthetic performers are sometimes used by advertisers to sell products, and with easy access to technology, there has been an increase in the use of AI-generated performers across all forms of media, including on social media and in digital advertising.
+L53: Without notice that the content the public is viewing is not real, AI-generated synthetic performers and manipulated media can undermine one's ability to accurately distill fact from fiction.
+L54: State Senator Michael Gianaris said, “Film and television production remains an integral part of New York’s economy, and that is why New York will continue to lead in protecting the workers who power this industry. As this legislation goes into effect, New York’s performers will be better protected from their likenesses being deceptively replaced by artificial intelligence, and we can hold accountable those who would take advantage of these tools to profit improperly at the expense of the real talent.
+L55: Thank you to Governor Hochul for enacting this important law.”
+L56: Assemblymember Linda B. Rosenthal (D/WF - Manhattan) said, “The rise of deepfakes and AI-generated performers have made it more difficult than ever for consumers to decipher fact from fiction. The synthetic performer legislation will alert New Yorkers to the use of synthetic performers in advertisements, providing much-needed transparency to consumers and protections to artists.
+L57: As companies rely on new marketing strategies to sell their products and services, consumers have a right to know if the person featured in those ads is real or fake and our first-in-the-nation law will ensure that happens."
+L58: SAG-AFTRA Chief Labor Policy Officer and New York Local Executive Director Rebecca Damon said, “SAG-AFTRA is grateful to Governor Hochul for placing New York at the forefront of developing smart guardrails around the use of generative AI. This Synthetic Advertisement Disclosure law protects consumers and workers from the risks posed by rapidly developing AI technologies.
+L59: The law’s enforceable protections mitigate performance replacement, prevent consumer deception, and affirm the continued value of human performance. As artificial intelligence technology evolves, we look forward to continuing to work with Governor Hochul on further AI guardrails.”
+L60: The enactment of synthetic performer law complements Governor Hochul’s ongoing efforts to ensure that the use of AI is for the common good. As technology continues to evolve, Governor Hochul remains committed to keeping New Yorkers safe online, and has implemented nation-leading regulations to ensure safe and responsible AI use in New York State. Initiatives include:
+L61:   * The SAFE for Kids Act and Child Data Protection Act that restrict addictive feeds for kids and prevent online operators from collecting and monetizing children’s data without informed consent.
+L62:   * AI Companion legislation which set first-in-the-nation safeguards, diverting user conversations about self-harm to mental health resources and interrupting unhealthy addictive behaviors. The Governor also outlawed AI-Generated Child Sexual Abuse Material.
+L63:   * The Unplug and Play Agenda which helps encourage healthy socialization and child development by funding social infrastructure, physical sites like playgrounds, community centers, and pools, and expanded youth programming.
+L64:   * New York’s Distraction Free Learning Policy which is already resulting in greater academic achievement, improved student wellbeing, and safer school environments for students.
+L65:   * The recently signed Warning Labels bill that will require social media companies post warnings about the platform's potential impact on mental health.
+L66:   * AI Deceptive Practices Act, which enhances protections against unauthorized use of likeness/voice and the unauthorized dissemination of intimate images.
+L67: This year, the Governor’s Safe by Design Act was implemented in the FY27 State Budget. Safe by Design ensures that parental controls for kids are set at the highest protections on common social and gaming platforms, which means that non-connections above the age of 18 cannot privately communicate with kids, view their full profile, or tag them in content. Location settings will also be turned off by default, and children under 13 must receive parental approval for new connections.
+L68: It also disables certain AI chatbot features on online platforms for kids and parents must be able to set limits on children’s financial transactions on online gaming platforms and view their child’s transaction history. While many of these platforms have increased their security features for kids, in New York it is now the law, and cannot be relaxed by these platforms over time.
+L69: Additionally, Governor Hochul is now creating a first-of-its kind Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity, and Trust (DIGIT). DIGIT will serve as a central, authoritative body for digital safety and technological governance, devising new approaches and ensuring consistent enforcement to keep New Yorkers safe online; while protecting New York’s position as a state that values and invests in cutting edge innovation.
+L70: The DIGIT Office will first focus on regulating large frontier AI developers, enabling greater transparency into their safety measures and establishing a reporting mechanism for developers to report critical safety incidents.

+L50: ## SECTION 396-B
+L51: 
+L52: ### Advertisements
+L53: #### General Business (GBS) CHAPTER 20, ARTICLE 26
+L54: § 396-b. Advertisements. 1. For the purposes of this section, the
+L55: following terms shall have the following meanings:
+L56: (a) "Artificial intelligence", "artificial intelligence technology",
+L57: or "AI" means a machine-based system that can, for a given set of
+L58: human-defined objectives, make predictions, recommendations, or
+L59: decisions influencing real or virtual environments, and that uses
+L60: machine- and human-based inputs to perceive real and virtual
+L61: environments, abstract such perceptions into models through analysis in
+L62: an automated manner, and use model inference to formulate options for
+L63: information or action. This definition includes but is not limited to
+L64: systems that use machine learning, large language model, natural
+L65: language processing, and computer vision technologies, including
+L66: generative artificial intelligence.
+L67: (b) "Generative artificial intelligence" means a class of artificial
+L68: intelligence models that are self-supervised and emulate the structure
+L69: and characteristics of input data to generate derived synthetic content,
+L70: including, but not limited to, images, videos, audio, text, and other
+L71: digital content.
+L72: (c) "Synthetic performer" means a digitally created asset created,
+L73: reproduced, or modified by computer, using generative artificial
+L74: intelligence or a software algorithm, that is intended to create the
+L75: impression that the asset is engaging in an audiovisual and/or visual
+L76: performance of a human performer who is not recognizable as any
+L77: identifiable natural performer.
+L78: 2. Any person, firm, corporation or association, or agent or employee
+L79: thereof, hereinafter called person, who, being engaged in the business
+L80: of dealing in any property, makes, publishes, disseminates, circulates
+L81: or places before the public or causes, directly or indirectly, to be
+L82: made, published, disseminated, circulated or placed before the public,
+L83: in this state, any advertisement respecting any such property, in any
+L84: newspaper, magazine, or other publication, or over any radio station or
+L85: television station, unless it is stated in any such advertisement that
+L86: the advertiser is a dealer in such property or from the context of any
+L87: such advertisement, it plainly appears that such person is a dealer in
+L88: such property so offered for sale in any such advertisement; or when
+L89: placing or causing any such advertisement to appear in any newspaper,
+L90: magazine or other publication or radio or television station as
+L91: described in this section, if requested by the publisher of any such
+L92: newspaper, magazine or other publication or owner or operator of such
+L93: radio or television station or any agent or representative thereof to
+L94: file with such owner or operator, publisher, agent or representative
+L95: thereof such person's true name, or where such person is transacting
+L96: business under a name other than the true name pursuant to law, then the
+L97: name under which such business is transacted, and each business address
+L98: wherein any business is transacted by such person, in the class of
+L99: property advertised or to be advertised for sale in such advertisement,
+L100: shall make any false statement in relation to any of such items; or if
+L101: requested by the publisher of any such newspaper, magazine or other
+L102: publication or owner or operator of such radio or television station or
+L103: any agent or representative thereof to file with such owner, operator,
+L104: publisher, agent or representative thereof a statement showing whether
+L105: such person is causing such advertisement to appear or is offering to
+L106: make such sale or disposition or transaction, as herein set forth, as
+L107: principal or agent, and if as agent, to set forth such information as is
+L108: specified in this section, in relation to such person's principal as
+L109: well as in relation to such person, shall make any false statement in
+L110: relation to any of such items; is guilty of a misdemeanor.
+L111: 3. Any person engaged in the business of dealing in any property or
+L112: service who for any commercial purpose produces or creates an
+L113: advertisement respecting any such property or service, in any medium or
+L114: media in which such advertisement appears, shall conspicuously disclose
+L115: in such advertisement that a synthetic performer is in such
+L116: advertisement, where such person has actual knowledge. A violation of
+L117: this subdivision shall result in a civil penalty of one thousand dollars
+L118: for a first violation, and five thousand dollars for any subsequent
+L119: violation.
+L120: 4. This section shall not apply to advertisements and promotional
+L121: materials for expressive works, including but not limited to, motion
+L122: pictures, television programs, streaming content, documentaries, video
+L123: games, or other similar audiovisual works, provided that the use of a
+L124: synthetic performer in the advertisement or promotional material is
+L125: consistent with its use in the expressive work.
+L126: 5. Nothing in this section shall limit, reduce, or enlarge any rights
+L127: any person may have under section fifty, fifty-f, or fifty-one of the
+L128: civil rights law or under any other law.
+L129: 6. Nothing in this section shall be construed to limit, or to enlarge,
+L130: the protections that 47 U.S.C. section 230 confers on an interactive
+L131: computer service for content provided by another information content
+L132: provider, as such terms are defined in 47 U.S.C. section 230.
+L133: 7. This section shall not apply to advertisements and promotional
+L134: materials in any of the following circumstances:
+L135: (a) Audio advertisements; or
+L136: (b) Where the use of artificial intelligence solely involves the
+L137: language translation of a human performer.
+L138: 8. Nothing in this section shall apply to any medium used for
+L139: advertising, including, but not limited to, newspapers, magazines, and
+L140: television networks and stations, streaming services, cable television
+L141: systems, billboards, and transit advertisements, by whom any
+L142: advertisement or solicitation in violation of this section is published
+L143: or disseminated.

+ def seekable(self):return True
+ def readable(self):return True

+ def seek(self,o,w=0):self.pos=o if w==0 else self.pos+o if w==1 else self.size+o;return self.pos

 ## The angle
 
-In beauty the line is not generated against shot, it is atmosphere against efficacy. Texture, packaging, ingredient stories, settings and casting can be generated; anything that shows what the product does to skin is a claim, and a claim needs the proof the regulator asks for. Map which assets sit on which side, market by market, with China as one market among four.
+Start with atmosphere versus efficacy, then test every factual visual claim. Packaging, shade swatches, texture and ingredient imagery also need product-specific verification; generation is not blanket clearance for those assets. Use generation for reviewed campaign illustration, preserve accurate product references, and never present invented on-skin results as evidence. Map asset choices and sign-off across the US, EU, UK and China.
